newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bomb suspects planned rush-hour attack - report.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bomb suspects planned rush-hour attack - report.

text.p: The men suspected of plotting to bomb New York City's subways planned the explosions for the Friday evening rush hour to attain maximum casualties in America's biggest city, a report said on Saturday.

The report, which appeared in the New York Post, was not confirmed by officials, who said a police raid on Thursday that led to the arrests of three men averted the attack by hours. The men have been linked to a radical Palestinian group.

"I think we were close to a disaster here, but it didn't happen. And that's the good news," said James Kallstrom, the head of the FBI in New York, said on Friday. "Whether it was 12 hours or 18 hours, 24 or 36 is irrelevant."
Two of men arrested were charged late on Friday as they lay in their hospital beds recovering from gunshot wounds suffered during the arrest.

As federal agents stood guard, a federal judge presided over the arraignment of Gazi Ibrahim Abu Mezer, 23, and Lafi Khalil, 22. They were charged with conspiracy to blow up a subway and possession of explosives.
The third suspect, not named by authorities, was being held on charges of being in the United States illegally, officials said.

The New York Daily News reported on Saturday that the man who tipped off authorities was an Egyptian, Abdul Rahman Mossabah, 31, who entered the United States only two weeks earlier after winning an immigration lottery. He was living with the suspected bombers, the News said.
"He was happy to be in this country and didn't feel this should happen to us," the source said. "He knew these guys were doing bombs to blow up people."
The FBI and the New York City police alleged in a joint statement that the suspects intended to target "U.S. and Jewish interests worldwide."
Sources also said the suspects made telephone calls to the Palestinian resistance movement Hamas from stores near the apartment in the residential Park Slope neighbourhood of Brooklyn.

"The suspects were using the telephones at the laundromat and grocery store near the apartment where they were staying and we were able to trace the numbers back to Hamas," one law enforcement source told Reuters.
Hamas denied any link, saying the group "does not consider the American people an enemy and it does not target any of its communities."
The New York Times reported that a portrait of Sheikh Omar Abdul Rahman, the Egyptian cleric convicted of plotting to bomb New York City landmarks, was found in the apartment of the suspects.

Police found an Arabic missive written by one of the suspects, Abu Mezer, which they interpreted as a suicide note and political manifesto, news reports said. The note reportedly stated his hatred for the United States and for the Jewish people.
Quoting unidentified sources, ABC News said the note also denounced the persecution of Arabs and expressed his support for Hamas.
In a leaflet faxed to international news agencies in Jerusalem, Hamas said the movement had repeatedly stated its rejection of attacks against targets other than Israel.
"Hamas targets only the Zionist occupation by its Jihad (holy war) and its battlefield is Palestine," the leaflet said.

A New York attorney for Moussa Abu Marzook, leader of the political wing of Hamas, said that his client called the suspects "cowboys" who were probably upset by the conditions of the Palestinian people.

"It's absolutely absurd," Stanley Cohen quoted Marzook as saying from Jordan, where he was deported in May after being held without trial for two years in a U.S. prison. "It's ridiculous and a total lie that Hamas had anything to do with these guys wanting to plant pipe bombs."
